response: **Verdict: LEGAL.** Alperen Vasquez goes out at $6,907,680 and Santi Lindqvist comes back at $6,559,211, comfortably inside the $6,907,680 ceiling we have to work with. That ceiling is dollar-for-dollar — 100% of outgoing salary — because our apron salary of $221,152,396 puts us over the first apron, where the friendlier 125%-plus-change band applies only to teams sitting below it. After the swap our apron salary lands at $220,803,927. Two things worth adding: taking back less than we send keeps us clear of any hard cap, and the savings, while real, leave us in exactly the same tier — this is a margin move, not a repositioning one. Anything that brought back even a dollar more than $6,907,680 would have failed the matching test outright.

Nowhere near the second apron — there is $15,373,151 of clearance below it. Apron salary comes in at $206,312,849: $200,512,849 of salary and likely incentives, plus $5,800,000 in unlikely incentives, which count toward the apron even though they stay out of cap and tax salary. Against the $200,428,000 tax line we are $5,884,849 into the tax, and we sit $2,702,151 under the $209,015,000 first apron. That first-apron figure is the one to manage: the second apron is a non-issue at this payroll, but $2,702,151 of room is thin enough that a single mid-tier signing or an unbalanced trade pushes us over it — and crossing the first apron costs us the full mid-level, the bi-annual, and access to the buyout market. The $5,800,000 of unlikely incentives is what ate that cushion, and it is the line item nobody thinks about until it bites.

The cleanest path is also the only real path: one salary out, large enough to cover $18,397,310, with nothing coming back. Apron salary is $226,221,310 against a $207,824,000 second apron, and being above that line strips the two tools that would normally make this easy — salaries cannot be combined in a trade, and cash cannot be sent. Terrance Rees at $29,255,111 does it alone with $10,857,801 to spare, and he is the least painful of the three by a wide margin. Bogdan Okoro at $46,733,476 clears by $28,336,166 and Kristaps Kearns at $51,551,674 by $33,154,364 — both massively overshoot, which means paying a premium in talent to solve a problem Rees already solves. All three figures assume a pure salary dump with zero coming back; the moment we accept salary into the deal, the required outgoing number climbs and the Rees option can stop working.

We are over the second apron, and barely — $711,815 over. Apron salary is $208,535,815 against the $207,824,000 second apron, and that margin is entirely manufactured by incentives: $203,535,815 of salary and likely incentives plus $5,000,000 of unlikely incentives that count for apron purposes only. Relative to the other lines, we are $20,640,815 past the $187,895,000 tax line and $12,590,815 past the $195,945,000 first apron. Practically, that $711,815 is the difference between having a taxpayer mid-level and having minimums only, and between being able to aggregate salaries in a trade and being frozen out of it entirely. With 13 players we still have roster spots to fill, and every addition pushes the number the wrong way — clearing $711,815 belongs at the top of the deadline list, because it is cheap to fix now and ruinous to ignore.

The second apron is $55,763,790 away, so that end of the ledger is irrelevant to us this season. Apron salary is $152,060,210, built from $148,760,210 of salary and likely incentives plus $3,300,000 of unlikely incentives that count only in the apron calculation. We sit $35,834,790 under the $187,895,000 tax line and $43,884,790 under the $195,945,000 first apron, which means the full toolkit is ours: the non-taxpayer mid-level, the bi-annual, expanded salary matching in trades, cash in deals, and the buyout market. The framing I would push on you is that room like this is an asset with an expiration date. With this much distance from the tax we can absorb another team's unwanted salary in exchange for draft compensation, which usually returns more per dollar than the open market does — and that room is worth the most at the deadline, when the teams above the aprons are desperate.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** The governing test is the 100%-of-outgoing rule that binds every team above the first apron: Elijah Novak's $40,483,226 goes out, so $40,483,226 is the most we may absorb, and Luka Reddish at $31,155,080 fits inside that with room left over. We start at an apron salary of $199,491,015, over the second apron, and finish at $190,162,869 — real money off the books in a tier where every dollar carries a punitive multiplier. Worth flagging: at $190,162,869 we remain above the second apron, but we are close enough that one more shedding move would restore aggregation rights and the taxpayer mid-level. That is the deal I would be hunting for next — this one is a down payment on it.

Good news first: the gap is $5,192,611, which is one rotation contract, not a franchise reset. Apron salary sits at $194,123,611 against the $188,931,000 second apron, and while we are above that line we can neither combine salaries in a trade nor attach cash, so the fix has to be a single contract going out with nothing coming back. **Verdict: ILLEGAL.** The blocker has nothing to do with money — we are carrying 15 players, which is the hard roster limit, so there is no slot for Brennan Kearns at $2,305,708 regardless of which exception we invoke. The minimum salary exception itself is perfectly sound at any apron level and would have worked here: we sit at $176,258,610 in apron salary, over the tax line, and the signing would take us to $178,564,318. Keep in mind that waiving a player leaves his full salary on the books as dead money, so the true cost of adding Kearns is his $2,305,708 plus whatever we are still paying whoever we cut — and at $178,564,318 those dollars are being taxed, not just spent.

The bill is $45,380,754. Tax salary is $213,916,137 against a $200,428,000 line, so we are $13,488,137 into the tax, and as a repeater that overage is priced brutally. The first $6,064,000 above the line runs at $3.00 per dollar, or $18,192,000. The next $6,064,000 runs at $3.25 per dollar, or $19,708,000. The last $1,360,137 falls into a bracket charging $5.50 per dollar and costs $7,480,754 all by itself. That is the slide to put in front of ownership: a $1,360,137 sliver of payroll generating $7,480,754 of tax is what repeater rates do at the margin, and shedding that sliver is the single highest-return move on the board. We also forfeit our share of the pool distributed to non-taxpaying teams, so the real gap between us and a team just under the line is wider than the $45,380,754 line item alone suggests.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** Kristaps Ferreira out at $6,495,294, Marcus Halvorsen in at $4,690,749, matching ceiling of $6,495,294 — the deal clears the only test that binds us, with margin to spare. We sit at $224,382,502 in apron salary, above the second apron, which caps incoming salary at a flat 100% of what leaves and limits us to one outgoing contract per trade. If the goal is to change our tier rather than trim the bill, we need a far larger salary dump than this.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** Two separate problems, and the first one is fatal on its own: at $199,092,091 in apron salary we are over the $188,931,000 second apron, and a team in that position may not combine two salaries in one trade. Isaiah Duval's $7,032,805 and Kobe Boateng's $5,164,503 add up to $12,197,308 of outgoing salary, but the rules forbid treating them as a single package — each has to stand alone. Even setting the aggregation ban aside, the money fails: $12,197,308 out means $12,197,308 is the ceiling on what comes in, and Brennan Reddish at $13,987,983 exceeds that by $1,790,675. The deal would also push us to $200,882,766, deeper into the tier that created the problem. If we want Reddish, the path is one outgoing salary of at least $13,987,983 — or getting under the second apron first, which fixes both violations at once.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** This one fails twice, and the second failure is what kills any attempt to redesign it. On matching: sending out $76,330,466 in Elijah Amadi and Bogdan Lindqvist buys a ceiling of $95,663,082 under the 125% + $250,000 formula that applies once outgoing salary clears $29,974,000, and Tobias Rees at $102,566,716 is $6,903,634 past it. On the hard cap: taking back more than 100% of outgoing salary hard-caps us at the first apron, $178,132,000, while aggregating two salaries hard-caps us at the second apron, $188,931,000 — when both trigger, the tighter number governs, so $178,132,000 becomes our absolute ceiling for the rest of the league year. The trade would land us at $203,776,026, or $25,644,026 above that ceiling. There is no version of this that works: even if we found another $6,903,634 of outgoing salary to satisfy matching, a hard cap at $178,132,000 leaves nowhere near enough room to house a $102,566,716 contract. We are at $177,539,776 today — a deal this size belongs to a team with cap space, not to us.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** Yes, Okoro is eligible: his pre-waiver salary of $13,200,000 sits below the $14,104,000 non-taxpayer mid-level, and that single comparison decides buyout-market access for a team in our tier. Our apron salary is $205,789,254, which puts us over the first apron — precisely the tier where the buyout restriction applies, and the reason this was worth asking. Had his old contract been written above $14,104,000, he would be off-limits to us for the balance of the season, so the margin here matters. Two practical notes: the roster is at 15, so a spot has to open before he can sign, and the only money we can offer at this payroll is the minimum. Teams under the first apron can come at him with mid-level dollars, which means eligibility and a realistic shot at landing him are two different questions.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** Deni Ibarra's pre-waiver salary of $35,400,000 sits far above the $14,104,000 non-taxpayer mid-level, and a team over the first apron is barred from signing any player waived during the regular season whose pre-waiver salary exceeded that figure. Our apron salary is $203,725,064, which puts us squarely in the restricted group, so this is a flat prohibition rather than a question of finding room — even a minimum deal for him is off the table. The test is his old salary, not what we would pay him, which is exactly the point of the rule: it exists to stop teams in our position from shopping the discard pile. Two things change this. He goes unsigned until the offseason, when the restriction lifts, or we get under the first apron before we sign him. With 14 players we do have room to add elsewhere — just not him.

Short answer: minimum contracts, and that is the entire list. Apron salary is $221,079,066 against a $207,824,000 second apron, and that position wipes out the whole exception menu — the non-taxpayer mid-level and the bi-annual both disappear above the $195,945,000 first apron, and the taxpayer mid-level, which survives the first apron, disappears above the second. The room exception was never in play; it belongs to teams operating with cap space, and we are $221,079,066 deep. The minimum salary exception is the lone survivor, available at any apron level and triggering no hard cap, so a 15th man and injury replacements remain doable. What this means for roster-building: with 14 players and only minimum deals available, every upgrade has to come through trade, and the second apron blocks aggregation there too. Plan on one-for-one swaps and veteran minimums as the toolkit for the rest of the year.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** This clears on the only test that binds us: Trey Nakamura's $48,984,062 goes out, the ceiling on what we may take back is that same $48,984,062, and Jalil Lindqvist at $40,940,761 sits well under it. This trade saves ownership money; it does not buy back flexibility, and if flexibility is the objective we need to move considerably more salary than this.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** Waiving and stretching Deni Petrov's $89,800,000 over the standard formula — twice the remaining year plus one, so three seasons — produces $29,933,333 of dead money per season, and that number alone blows past what the rules permit. The ceiling is 15% of the salary cap, which is $21,088,200 for 2024-25 (15% x $140,588,000), and it applies to all stretched dead money on the books at once, not to each contract separately. We already carry $14,700,000 of stretched money, so the combined figure would be $44,633,333 — $23,545,133 per season above the limit. For the waiver to work at all, Petrov would have to give back $70,635,399, which no agent on earth signs off on. The practical read: this contract cannot be stretched. If we want him off the roster, we either waive him outright and carry the full $89,800,000 against this season, or we find a trade partner — and at that number, that means attaching real draft compensation.

$62,395,410. That is the check, and here is how it gets there. We owe $59,079,856 on $15,978,883 of overage — the multiple there is what repeater status does to even a modest trip into the tax. Tax salary is $216,406,883 and the line is $200,428,000. Two options, and one of them is obviously right. $1,430,297. That is the number that should govern the rest of your offseason, because it is all the room we have below the $209,015,000 first apron. **Verdict: LEGAL.** We send out $11,849,122 in Julian Amadi and Zion Cordero, which under the middle-band formula — outgoing plus $8,527,000 — lets us absorb up to $20,376,122, and Micah Amadi at $16,949,667 fits comfortably inside that. The one thing to track is that a hard cap is absolute: no exception, no signing, no subsequent trade can take us a dollar over $195,945,000, so if we later want to absorb a big contract for draft compensation, that is the wall we will hit.

We are a taxpayer, but only just: the bill comes to $3,635,948. Tax salary is $191,530,948 against the $187,895,000 line, so we are $3,635,948 over, and all of it sits in the first bracket at $1.00 per dollar. We are on the standard schedule rather than the repeater schedule, which is what keeps the multiple at one — a repeater in the identical position would be paying several times this. Here is the part worth acting on. We are barely over the line, and getting under it eliminates the entire $3,635,948 and flips us from forfeiting our share of the distribution paid to non-taxpaying teams to collecting it. That is a two-sided swing considerably larger than the bill itself, and the price of capturing it is moving $3,635,948 of salary off the books. If ownership is asking about the tax, the honest recommendation is to duck under the line entirely — at this margin it is the highest-return move available to us.

The margin here is $629,894 — that is how far above the first apron we sit, and it is expensive for its size. Apron salary is $209,644,894 against a $209,015,000 first apron: $204,844,894 of salary and likely incentives plus $4,800,000 of unlikely incentives, and that incentive money is what put us over. Getting back under takes $629,894 — one minimum contract's worth of salary. Given what sits on the other side of that line, that is the most efficient move available to us this summer, and the first place to look is whether those unlikely incentives can be restructured or traded out.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** The overage is $1,390,481, which is frustratingly small but decisive. Micah Lindqvist's $12,452,393 goes out, and at $182,534,944 in apron salary we are over the first apron, which puts us on the strict 100%-of-outgoing matching rule — so $12,452,393 is the absolute ceiling on what we may absorb. Nikola Ibarra at $13,842,874 sits $1,390,481 past it. Three ways to save the idea: add a second small outgoing salary to raise the matching base, bring in a third team to route Ibarra's contract through, or ask the other side to trim his number. Note that even the fixed version takes us to $183,925,425, so we would be adding payroll in a tier where that carries a tax multiplier — I would want to be sure we value Ibarra well above Lindqvist before we spend the effort restructuring it.

Start with what we are forbidden from doing, because it narrows the field fast: we are at $237,373,529 against a $221,686,000 second apron, and above that line we may not aggregate salaries in a trade and may not send cash. So the $15,687,529 we need to shed has to leave in one contract, with nothing coming back. Four players do it alone. Luka Ibarra at $21,912,524 clears by $6,224,995 and Santi Achiuwa at $22,605,404 clears by $6,917,875 — both are efficient, in the sense that we pay close to the minimum talent price for the room we need. Tobias Ibarra at $57,736,350 clears by $42,048,821 and would be malpractice: that is a max contract solving a $15,687,529 problem. My recommendation is Luka Ibarra or Achiuwa with a sweetener attached, and I would start those calls now — the market for absorbing $21,912,524 of salary thins out badly as the deadline approaches, and every team with room knows exactly how much we need this.

The menu is short: the taxpayer mid-level and minimum contracts, and one of them comes with a string attached. Apron salary is $199,715,707, above the $195,945,000 first apron, which automatically eliminates the full non-taxpayer mid-level and the bi-annual — that happens the moment we cross the line, regardless of anything else. The room exception was never available to us; it belongs to teams operating with cap space. What survives is the taxpayer mid-level at $5,685,000 and the minimum salary exception. The taxpayer mid-level is the real asset, and using it hard-caps us at the $207,824,000 second apron for the remainder of the league year — a ceiling we could not exceed by a dollar for any reason, including a midseason trade or an injury replacement. At $199,715,707 we would still have room beneath it, but the hard cap would permanently take second-apron-crossing constructions off our board, so the question is whether a $5,685,000 signing is worth locking our ceiling for the season. Minimum contracts carry no such cost and stay available at any payroll.

The counterintuitive part first: we have the most financial freedom in the league and the shortest exception list. Because we are operating under the cap at $140,128,643, the mid-level exceptions are formally unavailable to us — a team with cap space spends its room first and then receives the room exception, $7,983,000, as the consolation. So the non-taxpayer mid-level at $12,822,000, the taxpayer mid-level at $5,168,000, and the bi-annual are all off our sheet, traded away for the ability to sign anyone up to the full extent of our space. The room exception at $7,983,000 goes live once that space is spent, and it triggers no hard cap. Minimum contracts are always there. The strategic warning: cap space is use-it-or-lose-it, and the room exception is smaller than the $12,822,000 mid-level we are giving up — so if we do not have a target we genuinely intend to sign, we are better off staying over the cap and keeping the mid-level. That decision has to be made before we renounce anything, and the $178,132,000 first apron and $188,931,000 second apron sit so far above us that neither factors into it.

Everything hinges on one constraint: the $22,420,621 we need to shed has to leave in a single contract. Apron salary is $211,351,621 against the $188,931,000 second apron, and the aggregation ban means packaging two mid-sized deals to get there is off the table — no combining salaries, no cash attached to grease the transaction. That leaves three candidates. Andre Brantley at $25,094,979 is the tightest fit, clearing by $2,674,358, and he costs us the least talent for the outcome. Goran Vasquez at $34,340,488 clears by $11,919,867 and Santi Petrov at $48,448,329 clears by $26,027,708 — both leave far more cushion than we need, which is another way of saying both overpay in talent for the same result. My advice is to build around Brantley, but understand that $2,674,358 of cushion is thin: we would need to commit to minimums for the remaining roster spots and avoid incentive-heavy additions the rest of the way. And whoever absorbs the salary will want draft compensation, so budget for that now rather than at the deadline when our leverage is at its worst.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** By $257,587 — the most annoying way there is to lose a trade. Andre Jokubaitis goes out at $6,398,457, and because our apron salary of $182,059,660 puts us over the first apron, our matching allowance is exactly that: $6,398,457, dollar for dollar with no cushion whatsoever. **Verdict: ILLEGAL.** The structure is dead before we even get to the money. At $225,624,263 in apron salary we are over the $207,824,000 second apron, and a team in that position may not combine two salaries in a single trade — Amari Osei's $11,040,033 and Jaylen Reddish's $8,865,910 cannot be packaged, period.
